items.title: Gym-Anything for Robotics: Scaling physical simulations with digital agents
items.snippet: Realistic, fast robotics simulations could enable large-scale training of embodied AI models that transfer to the real world. To address this, we introduce Gym-Anything for Robotics, a framework in which coding agents create realistic robotics simulations. Our core insight is that simulation creation is a coding agent task, so improvements in coding agents translate directly into richer and more faithful simulations. Using this pipeline, we build RoboWorld, a set of 25 simulations with 25 test and 175 training RL environments of varying difficulty.

items.title: Robot-Use Agents (RUA)
items.snippet: Notes on agents that operate a robot the way they operate a computer. A robot is a software system — drivers, middleware, planners, controllers — so a coding agent that can drive a codebase and a terminal can, in principle, drive an arm. The premise: a frontier coding agent already knows geometry, physics and programming, and a robot already exposes a programmable interface — so the policy can be written rather than learned, and then inspected, edited and debugged instead of retrained.

items.title: Evaluating large language models versus human therapists in generating interventions for patients with depression in psychodynamic psychotherapy
items.snippet: Objective: Recent advances in artificial intelligence, especially the rise of large language models (LLMs), hold great promise for transforming mental health care, but their growing integration also raises pressing questions about their ability to deliver meaningful therapeutic interventions. We developed an LLM-based framework composed of four specialized LLM agents, each representing a different therapeutic dimension, and a Judge-LLM that selects the most appropriate intervention for a given context.

items.title: Drift No More: Spectral Locking for Long-Horizon Open-Weight Multi-Agent AI
items.snippet: Long-horizon multi-agent systems suffer from three tightly coupled failures: task drift, role drift, and state staleness. We test the hypothesis that these share a common representational cause: agent hidden states move away from the directions encoding the active task, assigned role, and current shared state. We introduce ATLAS (Algebraic Task–role Locking with Adaptive Spectral Memory), a training-free intervention acting on hidden states before a token is generated.
